title: Chapter 51: Three Times Over, Part 4 of 5: Three Names
html:
He went then.
He went the way he had come, along his own straight line beside their footprints in the snow, setting each narrow shoe down exactly in front of the other. Corin heard him counting under his breath. Twenty-two. Twenty-one. Twenty. Past the first line of frozen sheets. Past the broken end of the iron bar, half buried. Toward the gate. Juno watched him go with her arms wrapped round herself. Silas watched him go with his hands in his coat pockets and his face set.
At the gate, he stopped.
He stood there with his back to them, very straight, in the gap where the gate stood half open on its sunken hinge. And he counted the bars. Corin could not hear him. But he saw the narrow black head move, very slightly, from one bar to the next. Eleven times.
Then he counted them again.
And then he did not count them a third time.
He turned round.
"There is a form," said Lucian.
His voice came back across the yard soft and clear, over the thudding of the presses through the wall. He did not come back across the snow. He stayed where he was, in the gap of the gate, with one hand on the cold iron and the other on the book.
"It is not an answer. You have had your three. It is a form that was not filled in correctly." A pause. "On Thursday, at the fourth bell, after the Saint Bride's paper, his Excellency asked me for a list. I made it that evening, from the Carriage Books and the Lady's consignment cards and the Bank's register of things weighed and held. I made it three times. I placed it before him on Friday morning."
"A list of what?" said Corin.
Lucian looked at him across the yard.
"Of every person," he said, "who has held, in their own hands, at any time in the last two years, a black wooden case. With a silver clasp. And a maker's mark on the clasp in the shape of a folded square."
The yard went very still.
Corin felt Juno's hand find his coat again. He felt Silas, at his other shoulder, take his hands out of his pockets.
Lot forty-one. A Lord's Last Evening. Taken whole, before the fire.
"There were three names," said Lucian. "The list was short. It was a small case, and not many people have held it, and it was always carried with great care. Three."
He said them the way he said everything. Separately. Each one set down by itself, like a coin on a table.
"Hale, L. Harvester. Retired."
Corin did not move.
"Thorne, C. Councillor's widow. By proxy."
Silas drew in his breath.
"E. Auditor. The Fourth Desk. Weighed and held, under clause eleven."
And Corin saw her. Quite suddenly. Not the way he saw the dead, in their last minutes, behind his eyes. The ordinary way. The way you see a face you have met. A woman in a dark green coat and white gloves, on a stair in the Bourse, coming down, with a lamp boy holding a lamp in front of her. With a gold front tooth that caught the light. With her eyes on him. Mind your leg, grandfather. He had not been able to stop on the stair. He had been on the ninth step, with his leg stuck out across it, and she had gone down past him. And afterward, Remy said, she had touched the blood he left there. She had knelt on the kitchen stair in her dark green coat and touched his blood with her bare fingers.
He did not know why that came into his head now. It just did. And with it, from somewhere very far down, a pool. And two braids. Cor, look—
He pushed it away.
"His Excellency read the list once," said Lucian. "He never reads anything twice. And then he took up his pen, and he made a mark beside one of the names. Only one. A small mark. A circle." His mouth pressed itself together. "He has used that mark before. On other lists. I know what it means. I copied the forms that came after."
"Which name?" said Corin.
He heard his own voice. It did not sound like his.
Lucian looked at him across the yard. For a long moment he did not answer. And Corin thought that he was not going to. That this was where the rule was. That a man who would only answer three questions, and had answered three, would not answer a fourth, even this one.
"The first," said Lucian.
Hale, L. Harvester. Retired.
Corin shut his eyes.
He saw a dark low taproom at the end of the Lantern Bridge, very warm, smelling of beer and wet coats and woodsmoke. And an old man in round spectacles in a chair by the fire, with a pot of tea at his elbow and his long fingers folded in his lap. Fingers that were stained blue to the second knuckle, from fifty years of the old harvesting inks. The man who had taught him everything. Who had taught him, when he was sixteen, how to hold a harvesting rod, and said, Gently, boy. Always gently. They have given enough. Who had sat in that chair in the autumn and lied to him, kindly, for an hour, and then, as Corin was leaving, put a hand on his coat as if to brush something off it, and slipped a key into the pocket. A key with a bow shaped like an oak leaf.
Master Linus Hale.
He's alive, then, Malakor had said, in the autumn. When Lucian's office sent the message down. Master Hale sends his regards. Corin had not known what Malakor meant. He still did not know.
He opened his eyes.
Lucian was still standing in the gap of the gate. He had not moved.
"I wrote that message," he said, as if he had heard Corin thinking it. "In the autumn. Master Hale sends his regards. For his Excellency, to be sent to you. I did not know what it meant. I copied it three times and sent it down the pipe." A pause. "I think now that it meant his Excellency knew Master Hale was still alive. And wanted you to know that he knew."
"When?" said Corin. "When is it—"
"I do not know." Lucian's voice was very low. "There is no form yet. There is only the circle. When there is a form, it will come up the pipe, and I will read it, and copy it. Three times." He looked down at the black book in his hand. "Sometimes the form does not come until after."
Then he turned round in the gap of the gate, sideways, and went through it.
Corin heard his narrow shoes on the stone of the tunnel. Quick and light and even. He heard him stop at the mouth of the arch, where the barrow stood with its FEVER card on its stick. He heard him say something, very quietly, to the barrow, or to the arch, or to nobody. Thirteen paces. The long way. And then the footsteps went on out into Quill Row, onto the black ice, and turned left, toward Sallow Steps, and the counting went with them.
"Two hundred and fourteen. Two hundred and fifteen."
And then it was lost in the thudding of the presses, and he was gone.
Nobody in the yard moved for a long time.
The frozen sheets hung above them on their strings, gray on gray, and the snow lay on top of each one in a thin white line, and they did not move either. Old Japhet's last sheets. Hung up to dry twelve years ago, the day before a strike, by a man who would not come out, and who went home that night and died in his chair.
"Linus Hale," said Silas at last, very low. "Your teacher."
"Yes."
"Where is he?"
"The Lamplighter's Rest. The inn on the corner of Ferrule Street, at this end of the Lantern Bridge. He has a room over the taproom, and a chair by the fire that nobody else sits in." Corin heard his own voice, flat and far away. "The step women went to warn him a week ago Friday, Bridie said, when they went to every door. He wasn't there. He'd gone out early. With his books."
"Then we warn him again."
"Yes."
"Tonight."
Corin looked at his leg. At the crutch. At Juno, standing on the sides of her wrapped feet in the snow with her face white and set. At Silas, who was to be collected tomorrow at the sixth bell by the Inquisitor himself.
"Tomorrow," he said. "First light. Bridie, or Marta. Someone with feet." He took a breath. "Tonight we've got to get back across the river before the barriers change. And I've got to tell Lyra that her aunt is on a list."
He looked at the gate.
"With a circle by somebody else's name," he said. "This time."
The Window on Ferrule Street
They did not mean to go past the Lamplighter's Rest. It was simply on the way.
The quickest road from Quill Row back to the Ministry Bridge, if you were pushing a barrow and did not want to go up and down the Sallow Steps, was along the embankment. Down through the bottom of the Ink Quarter, past the paper warehouses, to the river wall, and then along the river wall under the lamps, past the end of the Lantern Bridge, and on to the Ministry Bridge. Silas knew it. He pushed the dead along it every night. And Corin, lying under the gray blanket in the dark with Juno stiff beside him, knew it by the sounds. The presses fading. The river coming up, cold and brown. The wind off the water. And then, quite close, on the right, a great hollow booming of water through stone arches, seven of them, one after another, like a giant breathing.
The Lantern Bridge.
And on the left, at the corner where Ferrule Street came down off the embankment to meet the end of the bridge, the smell of beer, and woodsmoke, and wet coats. And a sound of voices, low, behind glass. And a fiddle, somewhere inside, playing very badly.
Silas stopped the barrow.
Corin did not know why at first. There was no voice calling out. No barrier. Then he felt the blanket lift, just a little, at the corner by his face. Silas's long fingers, holding it up. Making a gap.
"Look," said Silas, very low. "The window. On the left. Don't move."
Corin looked.
He saw the Lamplighter's Rest from below, from the level of the barrow, through the gap in the gray wool. A low old inn, built right into the corner, two floors and a steep roof, with its walls bowed out a little with age, and its timbers black, and its small square window-panes thick and green and full of bubbles, so that the light coming through them from inside was a soft wavering gold, like light through water. Over the door hung the sign. A lamplighter, painted, with his long pole on his shoulder and his little ladder under his arm, walking along a bridge of seven arches under a row of lamps. The paint was old and cracked. The lamplighter's face had worn away to nothing.
And in the window to the left of the door, the nearest window, there was a man.
He was sitting in a chair by the fire. Corin could only see him because the chair was close to the window, and the fire was behind him, and the light of it made a shape of him against the thick green glass. A small bent shape. An old man, in a dark coat, with a rug over his knees. Round spectacles, catching the firelight, two small gold circles. A pot of tea on a little table at his elbow. And a book open on his knees. A big book, with a dark cover. He was writing in it. Slowly. Corin could see the hand move across the page, and stop, and move again.
The hand was blue.
Not all of it. The fingers. To the second knuckle. Even through the thick wavering glass, in the gold light of the fire, Corin could see the color. Blue as ink. Blue as a winter evening. Fifty years of the old harvesting inks, the ones they did not use any more, that had soaked into the skin and stayed there.
Master Linus Hale.
Sitting in his chair by the fire, at the tenth bell on a Saturday night two days before Midwinter, writing in a book. With a circle by his name.
Corin did not move. He could not have moved if he had wanted to. He lay on his back on the barrow with his head turned to the gap in the blanket and looked at the bent shape in the green glass, and something in his chest closed up like a fist.
He had sat in that chair's twin, across the fire, in the autumn. In the afternoon. With the cold bright light outside and the dark inside. And the old man had poured tea with his blue fingers shaking a little on the handle of the pot, and talked to him for an hour. Kindly. And lied to him. Corin knew that now. Kindly, carefully, for an hour, the old man had told him nothing. And then, at the door, as Corin was leaving, he had put a hand on Corin's coat as if to brush something off it. You've got ash on you, boy. You always did. And when Corin got home that night and put his hand in the pocket, there had been a key there. Small and old, with its bow shaped like an oak leaf.
He still had the key. It was on a string round his neck, under his shirt, next to the Ledger. He had never found the lock.
"I could go in," said Silas, above him, very quietly.
Corin did not answer.
"I could go in," said Silas again. "I'm the parish doctor. I go into taverns. People send for me to taverns all the time, at this hour. Somebody's fallen down the stairs, somebody's been hit with a pot. Nobody would look twice." He paused. "I could go to his chair, and bend down, as if I were asking after his health, and say it. Five words. There's a circle by your name. And come out again."
Corin looked at the shape in the window.
At the blue hand moving across the page. Stopping. Moving.
"Yes," he said. "Go."
Silas put the corner of the blanket down. Gently. And Corin heard his long feet go away across the cobbles, and the door of the inn open, with a creak and a breath of warm air and noise, the fiddle louder, somebody laughing. And close again.
Then he lifted the corner of the blanket himself, with one gray finger, and watched.
He saw the tall thin shape of Silas come into the gold light behind the green glass. Saw it bend, the way a heron bends, over the small shape in the chair. He saw the blue hand stop moving on the page.
They were like that for a long time. Longer than five words. Corin could not hear anything. He could only see two shapes in wavering gold light, through thick old glass full of bubbles, one bent over the other. Like a painting of something. Like the sign over the door, with the face worn away.
Beside him under the blanket, Juno had lifted her own corner, and was watching too.
"He's not getting up," she whispered. "The old man. He's not running."
"No."
"Why isn't he running?"
Corin did not answer that.
Then the tall shape straightened. And the small shape in the chair turned its head.
Not to Silas. To the window.
It turned its head and looked out through the thick green glass, into the dark, at the street. At the end of the Lantern Bridge. At a fever barrow standing on the cobbles under a lamp, with a card on a stick that said KEEP BACK, and a gray blanket over two dead people, lifted a little at one corner.
Corin did not think the old man could see him. The glass was too thick and the light was wrong. He was looking out of a bright room into the dark. He could have seen nothing but his own face, and the fire behind him, and the room.
But he looked for a long time.
And then he lifted one hand. The blue one. Slowly, from the open book on his knees. And put it flat against the green glass of the window. Just for a moment. The way Elara had put her hand flat on the glass of the Fourth Desk window on Tuesday, Oren had said, looking down at the Bank steps. The way you put your hand on a door you are not going to open.
Then he took it away, and picked up his pen, and bent his head over the book again.
Silas came out a minute later.
He did not say anything until he had picked up the handles and pushed the barrow on past the end of the Lantern Bridge, under the lamps, along the river wall, two hundred yards, three hundred, until the fiddle and the voices and the gold light were gone behind them, and there was only the river and the wind.
Then he stopped, and put the handles down, and lifted the corner of the blanket off Corin's face.
"He knew," said Silas.
Corin looked up at him.
"He knew before I said it. I bent down and said, Master Hale, I'm the parish doctor of Saint Bride's, and I've come from Corin Vane, and there's a circle by your name. And he looked up at me over his spectacles and said, Yes, Doctor. Since Friday morning. Sit down a moment, you look perished." Silas's voice was strange. "He made me sit down. He poured me a cup of tea. With those hands. And he asked me how you were. How your hands were. How far the gray had got. And I told him. Past the wrists. And he said, Ah, very quietly, and shut his eyes."
"Why won't he run?"
"I asked him that." Silas looked away down the river. "He said, Where to, Doctor? I'm eighty-one. I've lived in that room for twenty years. Everything I have is in it. Everything I know is in this book. If I run, they'll take the book. If I stay, perhaps they'll only take me." He took off his spectacles. "And then he said to tell you something. He made me say it back to him twice, to be sure I had it."
"What?"
"Tell the boy I'll come tomorrow. To Saint Bride's. In daylight, with my stick, like an old man going to church on the Sunday before Midwinter, which is what I am. Tell him I'll come and say what I should have said to him in the autumn. And tell him to have his key."
Corin's hand went to his chest. To the string round his neck, under his shirt. To the small hard shape of an oak leaf.
"He said that," said Silas. "Tell him to have his key." He put his spectacles back on. "And then he picked up his pen and went back to his book as if I weren't there. And I came out."
He picked up the handles.
And Corin lay back under the blanket, in the dark, in the carbolic, with his gray hand closed round a small brass key through his shirt, and did not let go of it all the way to the Ministry Bridge.
